title: King, plus the man-to-woman arrow
hook: Can you do arithmetic with words? On the right map, king - man + woman lands somewhere.

knows: that a point on a map can stand for something
doesNotKnow: that models represent words as points (embeddings)
that directions in an embedding can carry relations

misconception: The computer stores each word's dictionary meaning, and similarity is looked up.
objective: The learner can explain that in a good embedding a relation (man to woman) is a direction, so an analogy can be answered by adding that direction to another word's position and finding the nearest word.

claims.text: The toy map's positions were placed by hand: man (0,0), woman (0,1), king (1,0), queen (1,1), crown (1,0.4), prince (1,-0.5).
claims.source: The lesson's own data in Demo.tsx (WORDS); the brief's coordinates, designed so the arithmetic is exact.

claims.text: On the toy map, king + (woman - man) = (1, 1), exactly queen; crown is 0.6 away and prince 1.5 away. Woman + (king - man) also lands on queen.
In real learned word vectors, such analogies hold only roughly.
claims.source: About real systems, from papers: Mikolov, Yih & Zweig 2013, 'Linguistic regularities in continuous space word representations' (NAACL-HLT), analogy accuracy well below 100%; Rogers, Drozd & Li 2017, 'The (too many) problems of analogical reasoning with word vectors' (*SEM), on the limits.

claims.text: Models represent words as points, and the nearest word to a computed point is the analogy's answer; nothing is looked up from a dictionary.
claims.source: Mikolov et al. 2013 (as c3): answers are found as the word whose vector is closest (cosine) to vec(king) - vec(man) + vec(woman), excluding the input words. The toy uses straight-line distance instead of cosine, a simplification.

recall.question: In a word map, the arrow from 'Paris' to 'France' is a direction. Add the same arrow to 'Rome'. Where should you look for the answer?
options: Anywhere: the arrow has no meaning away from Paris
recall.why: If a relation (capital to country) is a consistent direction in the map, carrying the arrow to another capital lands near its country. Real maps make this only roughly true.
